
## Introduction

This report investigates factors associated with employee ratings of their workplace. I will estimate and compare competing linear regression models, evaluate model diagnostics, and interpret the results of a preferred model.

## Data

```{r}
#| label: load-data

data("attitude", package = "datasets")

analysis_data <- attitude |>
  dplyr::select(rating, complaints, learning, raises)
```

The analysis uses the built-in R dataset `attitude`. The analysis dataset has 30 departments and four variables: overall workplace rating (`rating`), handling of employee complaints (`complaints`), opportunity to learn (`learning`), and raises based on performance (`raises`). The scores represent department-level percentages of favourable employee responses. So, each observation represents a department instead of an individual employee.

## Exploratory Data Analysis

### Descriptive statistics
### Descriptive statistics

```{r}
#| label: descriptive-statistics

descriptive_stats <- analysis_data |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Score"
  ) |>
  group_by(Variable) |>
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(Score),
    SD = sd(Score),
    Minimum = min(Score),
    Maximum = max(Score),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

descriptive_stats |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Descriptive Statistics",
    subtitle = "Department-level workplace attitude scores (n = 30)"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    SD = "Standard deviation"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(Mean, SD, Minimum, Maximum),
    decimals = 2
  )
```

### Distribution of workplace ratings

```{r}
#| label: rating-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of overall workplace ratings across 30 departments."

ggplot(analysis_data, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 8,
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_density(
    color = "navy",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Overall Workplace Ratings",
    x = "Overall workplace rating",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
### Relationships between ratings and predictors

```{r}
#| label: rating-complaints
#| fig-cap: "Overall workplace rating and handling of employee complaints."

ggplot(analysis_data, aes(x = complaints, y = rating)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    color = "steelblue"

    x = "Handling of employee complaints",
    y = "Overall workplace rating"

```

```{r}

  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,

  ) +

    title = "Workplace Rating and Learning Opportunities",

```

```{r}
#| label: rating-raises
#| fig-cap: "Overall workplace rating and raises based on performance."

ggplot(analysis_data, aes(x = raises, y = rating)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    color = "steelblue"

    title = "Workplace Rating and Performance-Based Raises",
```

### Summary of exploratory findings
Overall workplace ratings averaged 64.63 (SD = 12.17), ranging from
40 to 85 across the 30 departments. The histogram shows a main
concentration of ratings around the mid-60s, with a tail extending
toward lower ratings. All three predictors show positive associations
with overall workplace rating. Complaint handling has the clearest
approximately linear relationship, whereas learning opportunities and
performance-based raises show more scatter around their fitted lines.
There is no obvious strong curvature in these plots. Thus, linear
relationships is a reasonable starting point. Some departments lie
far away from the fitted lines, such as one with a learning
score near 58 and an overall rating of 40. During regression diagnostics, we would need to pay closer attention to these observations. The positive
associations are consistent with the expectation that more favorable
views of complaint handling, learning opportunities, and performance-based
raises accompany higher overall workplace ratings. Importantly, these department-level
associations do not establish causation.
## Model Specification
### Predictions

I expect that more favorable views of complaint handling will be associated
with higher overall workplace ratings because responsive and fair
handling of concerns may contribute to employees feeling heard and
supported. In addition, also predict that learning opportunities will explain additional
variation in workplace ratings beyond complaint handling, since
professional development represents a distinct aspect of the workplace
experience. Finally, I expect more favorable views of performance-based
raises to explain further variation after accounting for complaint
handling and learning opportunities, because recognition and perceived
fairness in compensation could contribute to overall workplace
evaluations. These expectations align with a sequence of models that
begins with complaint handling, adds learning opportunities, and then
adds performance-based raises. We will evaluate whether adding more predictors, such as pay, increases the fit of the model empirically.

### Competing regression models

I estimate four nested models, starting with an intercept-only baseline
and then adding complaint handling, learning opportunities, and performance-based
raises in this order.

```{r}
#| label: fit-models

# M0: Intercept-only baseline
model_0 <- lm(
  rating ~ 1,
  data = analysis_data
)

# M1: Complaint handling
model_1 <- lm(
  rating ~ complaints,
  data = analysis_data
)

# M2: Complaint handling and learning opportunities
model_2 <- lm(
  rating ~ complaints + learning,
  data = analysis_data
)

# M3: Complaint handling, learning opportunities, and raises
model_3 <- lm(
  rating ~ complaints + learning + raises,
  data = analysis_data
)
```
